Available agent types for the Agent tool:
- api-designer: Reviews REST and gRPC API design for consistency, correctness, and ergonomics. Checks naming, versioning, error codes, request/response schemas. Use when adding or changing API endpoints. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash)
- architect: Plans implementations before code is written. Use proactively before implementing features, bug fixes, or significant changes. Analyzes affected files, trade-offs, and risks. Returns a structured plan ready for the coder. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, AskUserQuestion, Write, Edit)
- ci-validator: Validates and fixes GitLab CI pipeline configs (.gitlab-ci.yml). Checks syntax, job dependencies (needs/stages), Docker image versions, cache config, and common failure patterns. Use when CI is broken or before adding new pipeline jobs. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash)
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)
- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)
- coder: Implementation specialist for Go, TypeScript/Next.js, and Python/FastAPI. Writes code following project conventions, runs the linter, and does NOT run tests. Use after architect produces a plan. (Tools: Read, Edit, Write, Glob, Grep, Bash)
- design-qa: Visual QA for layout, responsive design, and UI quality in aisyndicate (Next.js). Screenshots affected pages at mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), and desktop (1440x900). Use after UI changes to verify visual quality. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash)
- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- migration-planner: Plans database migrations safely for SQLAlchemy/alembic (syndicateclaw) and sqlite3 (SyndicateCode). Checks for data loss, concurrent write safety, and rollback strategy. Use before applying schema changes. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash)
- orchestrator: Orchestrates the full agent workflow — architect → coder → tester → reviewer → design-qa. Use for any feature, bug fix, or significant change. Returns a concise summary — all verbose agent output stays contained. (Tools: Agent, Read, Glob, Grep, Bash)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- reviewer: Reviews code changes for security, performance, readability, and consistency. Use proactively after code changes and tests pass. Returns categorized findings with actionable fixes. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash)
- security-auditor: Deep security audit for Go services, FastAPI, and Next.js. Checks auth flows, injection risks, data exposure, SSRF, and secrets. Use before shipping sensitive changes or on-demand. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)
- tester: The ONLY agent that runs tests. Writes, updates, and runs affected tests using go test, Playwright, or pytest. Loops with coder if failures are implementation bugs. Use after coder finishes. (Tools: Read, Edit, Write, Glob, Grep, Bash)

The following skills are available for use with the Skill tool:

- _gstack-command (gstack): Router for the gstack skill suite. (gstack)
- browse: Fast headless browser for QA testing and site dogfooding. (gstack)
- connect-chrome (open-gstack-browser): Launch GStack Browser — AI-controlled Chromium with the sidebar extension baked in.
- feature-engineering: Create and transform features using encoding, scaling, polynomial features, and domain-specific transformations for improved model performance and interpretability
- graphify: Use for any question about a codebase, its architecture, file relationships, or project content — especially when graphify-out/ exists, where the question should be treated as a graphify query first. Turns any input (code, docs, papers, images, videos) into a persistent knowledge graph with god nodes, community detection, and query/path/explain tools.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to self-pace. Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-mem:agent-cost-report: Believable agent cost report for any period, default the last 7 full days PT, not counting today. Measured tokens from Claude Code transcripts priced at OpenRouter list prices (ESTIMATED), measured provider spend when a sanctioned source exists, note-taker cost separate, Timing-style HTML/PDF plus report.json, line-items.csv, evidence.json.
- claude-mem:babysit: Watch a pull request or review cycle until it is ready to merge. Use when asked to babysit, monitor, or keep checking PR comments, reviews, and CI until all actionable issues are resolved.
- claude-mem:backup-setup: Set up, check, or restore local claude-mem database snapshots. Use when the user says "set up backups", "back up my memories", "backup status", or "restore my database".
- claude-mem:build: Fully automate a coding task with make-plan, do, and babysit.
- claude-mem:build-and-release: Fully automate building and releasing a coding task.
- claude-mem:ccs-align: Run the CCS Align seat's hourly breathing cycle — prove the local claude-mem worker is healthy, pull needle observations through search → timeline → get_observations, land them in a seat-owned middle cache via atomic grab → append → filter exclude-marks → replace, manage exclude marks, and walk house → project → seat rules to detect conflicts (SHADOW_HOUSE, DENY_ALLOW, DRIFT, CLOCK_HEADER) with an append-only rules-report.md. Use when asked to run CCS Align, breathe the alignment seat, refresh the middle cache, exclude or restore an observation, walk rules, check rules conflicts, or check the Worker Watch board.
- claude-mem:childhood: Babysit a shipped release after merge, publication, or deployment. Verify published packages, production behavior, installed plugins, and late CI or user reports until the observation window is clean; use babysit for PR readiness before release.
- claude-mem:cloud-sync: Set up or check claude-mem cloud sync with cmem.ai Pro. Use when the user says "set up cloud sync", "sync my memories", "cmem pro", "cloud backup", "sync status", or wants their memory database backed up or synced to their cmem.ai account.
- claude-mem:design-is: Audit a design against Dieter Rams' ten "Good design is..." principles, then hand off a /make-plan prompt for one of three outcomes — new design, refine design, or redesign. Use when the user says "audit this design", "design review", "check this UI against Rams", "is this UI good", "critique this design", "design audit", or asks for a critique that should lead to a plan.
- claude-mem:do: Execute a phased implementation plan using subagents. Use when asked to execute, run, or carry out a plan — especially one created by make-plan.
- claude-mem:handoff: Generate a HANDOFF.md that captures goal, current state, files touched, failed attempts, and next steps — so a fresh Claude session can continue exactly where this one left off. Use when sessions are getting long, Claude keeps retrying the same broken solution, or the user wants to step away and resume later.
- claude-mem:how-it-works: Explain how claude-mem captures observations, when memory injection kicks in, and where data lives. Use when the user asks "how does claude-mem work?" or "what is this thing doing?".
- claude-mem:knowledge-agent: Build and query AI-powered knowledge bases from claude-mem observations. Use when users want to create focused "brains" from their observation history, ask questions about past work patterns, or compile expertise on specific topics.
- claude-mem:learn-codebase: Prime a codebase by reading every source file in full. Use when starting work on a new or unfamiliar project, or when the user asks to "learn the codebase", "read the codebase", "prime", or "get up to speed".
- claude-mem:make-plan: Create a detailed, phased implementation plan with documentation discovery. Use when asked to plan a feature, task, or multi-step implementation — especially before executing with do.
- claude-mem:mem-search: Smart search (default). Search claude-mem's persistent cross-session memory database in three steps: search, timeline, then selected get_observations. Use when user asks "did we already solve this?", "how did we do X last time?", or needs work from previous sessions.
- claude-mem:mode-creator: Interactively create, install, activate, and verify custom claude-mem modes, including domain-specific observation types, concept tags, optional Telegram alerts, bot setup, worker restart, and startup-context verification. Use this whenever someone asks to customize what claude-mem remembers, create or change a mode, track domain-specific notes, add observation types or tags, or send Telegram notifications for particular memories—even if they do not use the word "mode."
- claude-mem:oh-my-issues: Cluster a GitHub issue backlog by root cause into a small set of plan-master issues, redirect children with a standardized comment, and bundle architectural-fix PRs that close clusters atomically. Use when an issue tracker has accumulated dozens of reports that share underlying defects, when asked to triage / consolidate / cluster / dedupe issues, when asked to build a plan series or roadmap from open issues, or when routing a new incoming bug into an existing plan.
- claude-mem:owner-goals: Map what the owner wants from the prompts they typed themselves (prompts an agent wrote are left out), then sort it into focus areas, asks and rules, each with dated quotes, and save them to My Work (areas as My Focus suggestions, rules as My Rules suggestions). Use when asked for "owner goals", "my goals", "what do I want", "what am I asking for", "map my prompts", or to refresh Goals in My Work.
- claude-mem:pathfinder: Map a codebase into feature-grouped flowcharts, identify duplicated concerns across features, and propose a unified architecture. Use when asked to "find the ideal path," unify duplicated systems, or audit architecture before a refactor. Emits a proposed unified flowchart plus per-system /make-plan prompts.
- claude-mem:release: Fully automate a release with version-bump and childhood.
- claude-mem:request-progress: Group recent conversations into overall requests, review each one's progress from memory, sort each into one of the owner's focus areas, and write the build story, so My Work shows progress meters, shipping velocity and learned working preferences. Use when asked to "group requests", "group by overall request", "review request progress", "refresh progress", "build story", "shipping velocity", or "how do I like to work with agents".
- claude-mem:screenpipe: Search screen and audio history recorded by Screenpipe and optionally save selected context into claude-mem. Use when the user asks to recall desktop activity, a meeting, or something seen in another app through Screenpipe.
- claude-mem:smart-explore: Token-optimized structural code search using tree-sitter AST parsing. Use instead of reading full files when you need to understand code structure, find functions, or explore a codebase efficiently.
- claude-mem:standup: Facilitate a read-only standup across git worktrees, branches, or PRs to compare changes and produce one consolidation plan.
- claude-mem:timeline-report: Generate a "Journey Into [Project]" narrative report analyzing a project's entire development history from claude-mem's timeline. Use when asked for a timeline report, project history analysis, development journey, or full project report.
- claude-mem:version-bump: Automated semantic versioning and release workflow for Claude Code plugins. Handles version increments across package.json, marketplace.json, plugin.json manifests, build verification, git tagging, GitHub releases, and changelog generation. npm publishing is done by the tag-triggered GitHub Actions workflow through npm trusted publishing.
- claude-mem:weekly-digests: Generate a serial week-by-week narrative digest of a project's full claude-mem timeline. Splits the timeline into per-ISO-week files, then runs one consecutive subagent per week — each receiving the prior week's carry-forward block — to produce one chapter per ISO week of data. Use when asked for "weekly digests", "week-by-week story", "serial timeline", or "narrative chapters" of a project's history.
- claude-mem:what-the: What the? Use when the user wants a plain-English breakdown of something technical — the who, what, where, why, and when.
- claude-mem:wowerpoint: Turn one document into a kawaii NotebookLM slide deck. Use for "wowerpoint this", "make a deck about <file>", "turn this report into slides", or any request to render a single document as shareable narrative slides.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option. - Use the max or ultra level only when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask for one, never on your own judgment: they are the costliest reviews and start many reviewer subagents.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Model-facing tool replies must be concise purpose-specific text; keep structured envelopes and internal metadata out of model context. Select only evidence useful to the current question, and expand from index to context to relevant details only as needed.

function packageJsonHasDependency(packageJsonPath: string, dependencyName: string): boolean {
  try {
    const packageJson = JSON.parse(readFileSync(packageJsonPath, 'utf-8')) as {
      dependencies?: Record<string, unknown>;
      devDependencies?: Record<string, unknown>;
    };
    return !!(
      packageJson.dependencies?.[dependencyName] || packageJson.devDependencies?.[dependencyName]
    );
  } catch {
    return false;
  }
}

export function getOpenClawGlobalSkillsDir(
  homeDir = home,
  pathExists: (path: string) => boolean = existsSync
) {
  if (pathExists(join(homeDir, '.openclaw'))) {
    return join(homeDir, '.openclaw/skills');
  }
  if (pathExists(join(homeDir, '.clawdbot'))) {
    return join(homeDir, '.clawdbot/skills');
  }
  if (pathExists(join(homeDir, '.moltbot'))) {
    return join(homeDir, '.moltbot/skills');
  }
  return join(homeDir, '.openclaw/skills');
}

export function isZCodeInstalled(
  homeDir = home,
  pathExists: (path: string) => boolean = existsSync
) {
  return pathExists(join(homeDir, '.zcode')) || pathExists('/Applications/ZCode.app');
}

export function isKimchiInstalled(
  homeDir = home,
  pathExists: (path: string) => boolean = existsSync
) {
  return pathExists(join(homeDir, '.config', 'kimchi'));
}

export function isMiniMaxCodeInstalled(
  homeDir = home,
  pathExists: (path: string) => boolean = existsSync
) {
  return pathExists(join(homeDir, '.minimax')) || pathExists('/Applications/MiniMax Code.app');
}

export function isPositAssistantInstalled(
  homeDir = home,
  pathExists: (path: string) => boolean = existsSync
) {
  // ~/.positai is the pre-rename config dir, still present on installs
  // that haven't launched a current version yet.
  return pathExists(join(homeDir, '.posit/assistant')) || pathExists(join(homeDir, '.positai'));
}

## Project Overview

`skills` is the CLI for the open agent skills ecosystem.

## Commands

| `skills add <pkg>`            | Install skills from git repos, URLs, or local paths |
| `skills use <pkg>@<skill>`    | Use one skill without installing                    |
| `skills experimental_install` | Restore skills from skills-lock.json                |
| `skills experimental_sync`    | Sync skills from node_modules into agent dirs       |
| `skills list`                 | List installed skills (alias: `ls`)                 |
| `skills update [skills...]`   | Update skills to latest versions                    |
| `skills init [name]`          | Create a new SKILL.md template                      |

Aliases: `skills a` works for `add`. `skills i`, `skills install` (no args) restore from `skills-lock.json`. `skills ls` works for `list`. `skills experimental_install` restores from `skills-lock.json`. `skills experimental_sync` reads skills from npm dependencies (`sync` remains a compatibility alias).

## Update Checking System

### How `skills check` and `skills update` Work

1. Read `~/.agents/.skill-lock.json` for installed skills
2. Filter to GitHub-backed skills that have both `skillFolderHash` and `skillPath`
3. For each skill, call `fetchSkillFolderHash(source, skillPath, token)`. Tree requests start anonymously, then use an explicit `GITHUB_TOKEN`/`GH_TOKEN`, then `gh api` without exporting the GitHub CLI credential.
4. `fetchSkillFolderHash` calls the GitHub Trees API (`/git/trees/<branch>?recursive=1` for `main`, then `master` fallback); update checks fall back to an authenticated Git clone when API access is unavailable.
5. Compare latest folder tree SHA with lock file `skillFolderHash`; mismatch means update available
6. `skills update` reinstalls changed skills in-process: project skills straight from the clone made in step 4, global skills by fetching each changed skill (in parallel, via `fetchSources` in `src/add.ts`) and writing it with `installFetched`. Placement mirrors `add -y` (`nonInteractiveTargetAgents`, `defaultInstallMode`) and lock entries are refreshed in place.

### Lock File Compatibility

The lock file format is v3. Key field: `skillFolderHash` (GitHub tree SHA for the skill folder).

If reading an older lock file version, it's wiped. Users must reinstall skills to populate the new format.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# End-to-end matrix: patched upstream Skills CLI installs with --agent nexus; Nexus loads the result.
# Every case uses a fresh HOME and project dir; the developer's real skill dirs are never touched.
set -u
SP=/tmp/claude-1000/-home-mike-nexus-code/575fdc5c-0980-467b-a238-8f673c2cf4b3/scratchpad
SKILLS="node $SP/upstream/skills/bin/cli.mjs"
DIST=${DIST:-/home/mike/nexus-wt/agent-skills-vercel/cli/dist}
PROBE="node $SP/matrix/probe.mjs $DIST"
export DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 DO_NOT_TRACK=1
fresh() { H=$(mktemp -d "$SP/matrix/home.XXXX"); P=$(mktemp -d "$SP/matrix/proj.XXXX"); export HOME=$H; unset XDG_CONFIG_HOME XDG_DATA_HOME XDG_STATE_HOME; mkdir -p "$H/.nexus"; }
FIX=$SP/matrix/fixture-repo
rm -rf "$FIX"; mkdir -p "$FIX/skills/demo-skill" "$FIX/skills/folded-skill"
printf -- '---\nname: demo-skill\ndescription: Demo skill for the Nexus matrix\nallowed-tools: Bash(*)\n---\n\n# Demo\n\nSay DEMO.\n' > "$FIX/skills/demo-skill/SKILL.md"
printf -- '---\nname: folded-skill\ndescription: >\n  Folded description\n  over two lines\nmetadata:\n  name: impostor\n---\n\nBody\n' > "$FIX/skills/folded-skill/SKILL.md"

echo "== M1 detection: nexus is detected and listed as Nexus Code"; fresh
(cd "$P" && $SKILLS add "$FIX" --agent not-an-agent -y 2>&1 | grep -o 'Valid agents:.*' | tr ',' '\n' | grep -x ' nexus' )
(cd "$P" && node -e 'import("'"$SP"'/upstream/skills/src/agents.ts").then(async m=>console.log("detected:",(await m.detectInstalledAgents()).includes("nexus"),"displayName:",m.agents.nexus.displayName))')

echo "== M2 project install --agent nexus (untrusted, then trusted workspace)"; fresh
(cd "$P" && $SKILLS add "$FIX" --agent nexus -y >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "exit=$?"; find .agents -name SKILL.md | sort)
$PROBE "$P"; $PROBE "$P" trust

echo "== M3 global install -g --agent nexus"; fresh
(cd "$P" && $SKILLS add "$FIX" -g --agent nexus -y >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "exit=$?"); (cd "$H" && find .agents -name SKILL.md | sort)
$PROBE "$P"

echo "== M4 symlink (--link style) project install via another agent's dir + list/remove"; fresh
(cd "$P" && $SKILLS add "$FIX" --agent nexus claude-code -y >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "exit=$?"; ls -la .claude/skills 2>/dev/null | grep -- '->' | sed 's/.*:[0-9][0-9] //')
$PROBE "$P" trust | grep -c '"name"'
(cd "$P" && $SKILLS list --agent nexus 2>&1 | grep -E 'demo-skill|folded-skill' | sed 's/\x1b\[[0-9;]*m//g' | head -4)
(cd "$P" && $SKILLS remove demo-skill --agent nexus -y >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "remove exit=$?"; find .agents -name SKILL.md | sort)
$PROBE "$P" trust | grep '"name"'

for pkg in vercel-labs/agent-skills anthropics/skills; do
  echo "== M5 public package $pkg (project, --agent nexus)"; fresh
  (cd "$P" && $SKILLS add "$pkg" --agent nexus --skill '*' -y >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "exit=$?"; echo "installed: $(find .agents -name SKILL.md | wc -l)")
  $PROBE "$P" trust | node -e 'let s="";process.stdin.on("data",d=>s+=d).on("end",()=>{const o=JSON.parse(s);console.log("loaded:",o.trusted.length,"untrusted:",o.untrusted.length,"badDescriptions:",JSON.stringify(o.badDescriptions))})'
done

1:# Skills and Plugins Guide
2:
3:Nexus Code provides two distinct extensibility mechanisms:
4:1. **Agent Skills (`SKILL.md`)**: Reusable domain knowledge, procedural guidelines, and prompt instructions that the agent discovers and loads dynamically.
5:2. **JavaScript Plugins (`.js`)**: Dynamic runtime extensions that hook into agent lifecycle events and register custom executable tools.
6:
7:---
8:
9:## 1. Agent Skills
10:
11:Skills allow Nexus Code to adopt specialized expert personas and workflows on demand without permanently bloating the system prompt.
12:
13:### Discovery Locations
14:Skills are automatically discovered from:
15:- Current workspace: `./skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` or `./.nexus/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md`
16:- User global skills: `~/.nexus/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md`, `~/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md`, or `~/.config/opencode/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md`
17:
18:### Creating a Skill
19:Create a directory with a `SKILL.md` containing YAML frontmatter:
20:
21:```markdown
22:---
23:name: react-refactor
24:description: Guidelines for refactoring React components to functional hooks with TypeScript
25:---
26:
27:# React Refactoring Guidelines
28:
29:When refactoring React class components or legacy JSX:
30:1. Convert class components into functional components using React.FC.
31:2. Replace lifecycle methods with `useEffect` and `useCallback`.
32:3. Extract inline state into custom hooks when state logic exceeds 20 lines.
33:4. Verify tests pass with `npm test`.
34:```
35:
36:### Inspecting and Activating Skills
37:In the REPL:
38:- `/skills`: List all discovered skills.
39:- `/skill react-refactor`: Display full skill instructions.
40:The autonomous agent can also load skills dynamically during execution via the `activate_skill` tool.
41:
42:---
43:
44:## 2. Dynamic JavaScript Plugins
45:
46:Plugins are standard JavaScript ES modules placed in:
47:- `~/.nexus/plugins/*.js`
48:- `~/.config/opencode/plugins/*.js`
49:- `./.nexus/plugins/*.js`
50:
51:### Plugin Structure
52:A plugin exports a default object:
53:
54:```javascript
55:export default {
56:  name: "metric-logger",
57:  description: "Logs timing metrics and custom alerts for builds",
58:
59:  // Lifecycle Hooks

cd /home/mike/nexus-wt/agent-skills-vercel && python3 - <<'EOF'
p='docs/SKILLS_AND_PLUGINS.md'; s=open(p).read()
old='''### Discovery Locations
Skills are automatically discovered from:
- Current workspace: `./skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` or `./.nexus/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md`
- User global skills: `~/.nexus/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md`, `~/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md`, or `~/.config/opencode/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md`
'''
assert s.count(old)==1
new='''### Discovery Locations
Skills are discovered from these directories, each holding `<skill-name>/SKILL.md`. When two skills share a name, the first location in this order wins:

1. User global skills, always loaded: `~/.nexus/skills`, `~/.config/nexus/skills`, `~/.agents/skills`, `~/.config/opencode/skills`, `~/.claude/skills`
2. Current workspace, loaded only when the workspace is trusted (`nexus trust .`): `./.nexus/skills`, `./.agents/skills`, `./.claude/skills`, `./skills`

A workspace skill can never replace a user global skill of the same name. In an untrusted workspace, workspace skills are listed as untrusted and `activate_skill` refuses them.

Symlinked skill directories are followed, so a skill linked from another location loads normally.

### Installing skills with the Agent Skills CLI
`.agents/skills` (project) and `~/.agents/skills` (global) are the shared Agent Skills directories. Any installer that writes there works with Nexus. With the open-source [Skills CLI](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills), installing into those directories for another agent that shares them also makes the skills available to Nexus. For example, `--agent codex` writes to the same directories.

A `nexus` agent entry ("Nexus Code") for that CLI has been prepared but is **not yet part of a released Skills CLI**. Until it is, `npx skills add <owner/repo> --agent nexus` is rejected as an unknown agent.

Treat an installed skill as untrusted instructions. Activating a skill only adds its text to the conversation. Its frontmatter is read for `name` and `description` alone: keys such as `allowed-tools` grant nothing, and every tool call the skill suggests still goes through Nexus's normal approval, filesystem and execution policy.
'''
s=s.replace(old,new)
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

  other key grant nothing.
